::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Status: design. No probe has run.

Written against [the design standard](../studies/DESIGN-STANDARD.md). The author maintains
retraction trackers (XeraRetractionTracker, RetractionPollution) that study post-retraction
citation, reasons and geography. Acceptance speed is not among what they cover.
:::

## 1. The question

A paper mill needs its product accepted, and a manipulated or absent peer review is quick. If
that mechanism is real, a short time from submission to acceptance should be associated with
retraction for misconduct, and not with retraction for honest error, which has no reason to
depend on review speed. The second half is what makes this a test rather than a correlation.

## 2. Prior work, and the search behind the novelty claim

Log key `P17`.

```
corpus regex: (peer review (time|duration|speed)|time to acceptance|acceptance (time|interval)
              |submission.to.acceptance).{0,80}(retract|misconduct|paper mill)
PubMed:       ("time to acceptance"[tiab] OR "submission to acceptance"[tiab]
              OR "peer review duration"[tiab] OR "review time"[tiab] OR "acceptance time"[tiab])
              AND (retract*[tiab] OR "paper mill*"[tiab] OR misconduct[tiab])
```

Seven PubMed records, none in the corpus. The closest is a study of publication speed and
retraction among COVID-19 articles (PMID 35432503), and a study of retracted chemistry manuscripts
by error versus misconduct (PMID 37692206). This design extends the speed question beyond one
pandemic topic and adds the reason contrast, which is the part that tests a mechanism.

## 3. Hypothesis

A shorter submission-to-acceptance interval is associated with retraction for misconduct-class
reasons, and not with retraction for honest-error reasons.

**Null.** The odds ratio per halving of the interval is 1 for misconduct-class retractions.

**What would falsify it.** An odds ratio at or below 1 for misconduct, or an association of the
same size for honest error, which would mean speed marks something about the journal rather than
about the fraud.

## 4. Design and unit

Matched case-control, run twice: once with misconduct-class cases, once with honest-error cases,
each with its own controls. One article is one unit.

## 5. Sample

**Cases**: articles in Retraction Watch with `RetractionNature` equal to Retraction, a DOI and a
PMID, and PubMed History dates for both received and accepted. Classified into misconduct-class
(paper mill, fake peer review, fabrication, falsification, plagiarism, manipulated images) and
honest-error class (error in data, analysis or results by the authors, with no misconduct reason)
using Retraction Watch's reason codes, with the mapping published before classification.

**Controls**: four per case, from the same journal and the same publication month, not in
Retraction Watch, with both History dates. Sampled without replacement; a case with fewer than
four eligible controls keeps those it has and the set is weighted (S9).

## 6. Exposure

Days from received to accepted, from PubMed `History/PubMedPubDate` with `PubStatus` "received"
and "accepted", using full dates (S7). Analyzed on the log scale.

## 7. Outcome

Case or control status, by reason class.

## 8. Validation gate

Reason-class mapping is checked by the author on 150 cases against the retraction notices
themselves. **Below 90 percent agreement on the two classes, the mapping is revised and the check
repeated before any model is fitted.**

## 9. Analysis

In R.

```r
clogit(case ~ log2(days_to_accept) + strata(match_set), data = d)
```

Fitted separately for each reason class; the contrast between the two coefficients is the test.
Preregistered alongside: a model with the interval in categories, and one excluding special
issues, where editorial handling differs.

## 10. Threats

| threat | handling | removed or disclosed | standard |
|---|---|---|---|
| History dates are missing for many publishers | Complete-case within matched sets; missingness reported by publisher | Disclosed | |
| Misconduct retractions cluster in a few journals | Matching on journal and month holds the journal constant | Removed | S9 |
| Reason codes are Retraction Watch's, not the publisher's | Mapping checked against notices on 150 cases | Disclosed | S8 |
| Retraction lag means recent fraud is not yet retracted | Cases are what has been retracted; biases toward the null | Disclosed | S10 |
| Same-day received and accepted dates are a data artifact | Flagged and analyzed separately rather than entered as zero | Disclosed | S7 |

## 11. Probes

| probe | computes | goes to | what would change the design | status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **PA** | proportion of retracted and of all PubMed articles with both History dates, by publisher | 5 | under 40 percent coverage among cases makes the sample unrepresentative of retractions | not run |
| **PB** | case counts per reason class after the date requirement | 5 | fewer than 300 honest-error cases makes the contrast imprecise | not run |
| **PC** | the author's 150 reason checks | 8 | below 90 percent the mapping is revised | needs the author |

## 12. What this cannot show

- That fast review caused anything. Journals that review quickly may simply attract fraud.
- Anything about fraud that has not been retracted.
